All of our participants reported good or very good physical health.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

#### Issues Identified

48 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 2 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

This study was approved by the We recruited participants who were planning to retire or who had retired recently.
Prior to interviews, participants filled out a questionnaire to report their demographics.

Several measures were in place to ensure confidentiality; all participants were asked to not share personal information during the interview, with focus group participants using anonymous ID to refer to one another.
After each interview participants were debriefed, and interviewers completed reflexivity statements, documenting prior assumptions about the participant and reflections on the interview interaction.

There were 16 men (69.6%) and seven women (30.4%), and all were born and residing in the United Kingdom; our participants were recruited from local areas, including Newcastle, Sunderland, Darlington, and Durham 2 .
Most participants were married (82.6%) and everyone was living with others in their household.
All of our participants reported good or very good physical health.

Among those retired, 13 had retired within the 3 months before the interviews, consistent with our inclusion criteria; two participants who had been retired longer (8 months and 2 years) were also included.
When such structure was gone, even after retirement, our participants continued having to negotiate, protect and justify autonomy and ownership over their time.

(ID: 25; 59 years old, planning to retire in 3 months) For some of our participants, it can be difficult to adapt to the routine of less work and more alone time, especially at the start of retirement.

Complementing the previous theme that suggests life after retirement meant reclaim ownership over one's time, many of our participants expressed interests in self-improvement activities, reflecting a positive outlook toward aging.
Through reflection, participants were able to identify what mattered to them and direct their time toward enjoyable activities, personal interests, and their own happiness.

Theme 3: Retirees may face several obstacles in adjusting to life after retirement Sub-theme 3.1: Financial security (or its absence) shapes retirees' ability to plan for and enjoy retirement without worry Finally, after having reflected on all the positives and negatives that might come with retirement and the increased time for solitude, our participants identified a few obstacles that might prevent them from fully embracing their retirement.
The insight we have learned from these interviews is that all of our participants had something meaningful to say about their time alone.
For our participants, a lot of these pursuits were tied to time spent alone, especially for those whose partners were still at work.
All of our participants also reported good or very good physical health, and most had higher life satisfaction.

Fourteen of our 15 retired participants had therefore retired before State Pension age, suggesting that they may have had other resources to rely on before reaching 66, such as private pensions, savings, or a spouse's earnings (Cribb, 2023).

text.text: Retirement marks a significant life transition, often accompanied by the loss of daily routines, and subsequently, an increase in alone time.
This study interviewed 8 pre-retirees and 15 retirees living in the United Kingdom using semi-structured interviews.

Guided by the Theory of Planned Behavior, we asked participants to reflect on their attitudes toward solitude, other people's judgement of their time alone, and their perceived control over managing solitude.

Reflexive thematic analysis identified three themes: renegotiating boundaries with past work ties and family to make space for new personal pursuits; solitude as both an opportunity for personal growth and a potential risk of boredom and isolation; and financial security and health as important catalysts to adjustment.

Findings suggest that positive experiences of solitude depend not only on attitudes toward time alone, but also on protecting that time and having the routines, social connections, and resources to use it well.
Retirement marks a major shift in daily structure, identity, and social roles (Hopkins et al., 2006; Ingale & Paluri, 2025; Loureiro et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Retirement marks a major shift in daily structure, identity, and social roles <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Hopkins et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Ingale & Paluri, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Loureiro et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Around the world, particularly in European countries, Canada and the United States, more people are exiting work earlier than their country's retirement age (Khan & Dander, 2023).
text.formatted: Around the world, particularly in European countries, Canada and the United States, more people are exiting work earlier than their country's retirement age <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Khan & Dander, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Freed from workplace obligations, retirees face not only changes in financial situation but also shifts in roles and daily routines (Ingale & Paluri, 2025).
text.formatted: Freed from workplace obligations, retirees face not only changes in financial situation but also shifts in roles and daily routines <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Ingale & Paluri, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: How individuals cope with this transition also depends on individual preferences, resources, and life circumstances (Jonsson et al., 2000; Pettican & Prior, 2011).
text.formatted: How individuals cope with this transition also depends on individual preferences, resources, and life circumstances <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Jonsson et al., 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Pettican & Prior, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Some find retirement deeply satisfying, reporting greater well-being, autonomy, and time for personal interests (Gorry et al., 2018; Stanley et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Some find retirement deeply satisfying, reporting greater well-being, autonomy, and time for personal interests <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Gorry et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Stanley et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Others struggle with boredom, purposelessness, or heightened awareness of social losses (Ugwu et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Others struggle with boredom, purposelessness, or heightened awareness of social losses <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">(Ugwu et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Retirement also brings a significant shift in time use, with implications for health and wellbeing.

Retirees often replace time spent working or commuting with television or other sedentary activities (Olds et al., 2018; Touvier et al., 2010; Van Dyck et al., 2016), and opportunities for physical activity may be limited, particularly for those who are older or in poor health (Stenholm et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Retirees often replace time spent working or commuting with television or other sedentary activities <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Olds et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Touvier et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Van Dyck et al., 2016)</ref>, and opportunities for physical activity may be limited, particularly for those who are older or in poor health <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Stenholm et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: While most studies focused on time spent on leisure and physical activities after retirement, in this study we focused on older adults' thinking and experiences with solitude during this transition.

Time-use data consistently show that older adults spend more of their day alone (Larson, 1990; Peplau & Perlman, 1982; Toyoshima & Sato, 2019), partly because of changes in social relationships (e.g., losing co-workers) and daily routines (i.e., no longer going to work) (Jonsson et al., 2000; Pettican & Prior, 2011).
text.formatted: Time-use data consistently show that older adults spend more of their day alone <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Larson, 1990;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Peplau & Perlman, 1982;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">Toyoshima & Sato, 2019)</ref>, partly because of changes in social relationships (e.g., losing co-workers) and daily routines (i.e., no longer going to work) <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Jonsson et al., 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Pettican & Prior, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: This makes extended solitude a particular risk for loneliness in later life (Danvers et al., 2023).
text.formatted: This makes extended solitude a particular risk for loneliness in later life <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Danvers et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: It is important to highlight the conceptual distinctions between solitude and related concepts like loneliness and isolation, particularly in the context of retirement.

It has been shown that children as young as eleven recognize that solitude is different from loneliness (Galanaki, 2004), and academic communities have also recognized this distinction (Nguyen & Rodriguez, 2024).
text.formatted: It has been shown that children as young as eleven recognize that solitude is different from loneliness <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Galanaki, 2004)</ref>, and academic communities have also recognized this distinction <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Nguyen & Rodriguez, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Solitude refers to the state of being detached from social engagement, either in person or remotely (i.e., not speaking with someone on the phone nor interacting with others via text messages or social media platforms).

On the other hand, loneliness is a subjective experience arising from unmet social needs, and social isolation is an objective condition of not having access to social contact or a wider social network.

While solitude, loneliness, and social isolation may co-occur, loneliness can also be experienced in the presence of others, and a person may be alone temporarily while still maintaining access to other people.
Loneliness in older populations has been tied more to life circumstances or health conditions (Hawkley & Cacioppo, 2007) than to objective lack of social interactions (Hawkley et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Loneliness in older populations has been tied more to life circumstances or health conditions <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Hawkley & Cacioppo, 2007)</ref> than to objective lack of social interactions <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Hawkley et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: For example, bereavement, reduced mobility, and the loss of social networks can all heighten the risk of both isolation and loneliness (Courtin & Knapp, 2017; Hawkley & Cacioppo, 2007; Victor & Bowling, 2012).
text.formatted: For example, bereavement, reduced mobility, and the loss of social networks can all heighten the risk of both isolation and loneliness <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Courtin & Knapp, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Hawkley & Cacioppo, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">Victor & Bowling, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: On the other hand, older adults who spend more time alone are not necessarily lonely and isolated; even in the absence of regular social interactions, older adults with strong social networks continue to enjoy the emotional benefits of solitude (Pauly et al., 2018).
text.formatted: On the other hand, older adults who spend more time alone are not necessarily lonely and isolated; even in the absence of regular social interactions, older adults with strong social networks continue to enjoy the emotional benefits of solitude <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Pauly et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, the common but mistaken assumption that time in solitude necessarily leads to loneliness and isolation may be explained by third variables, such as living alone, being widowed, having no (surviving) children, or worsening health (Grenade & Boldy, 2008).
text.formatted: Therefore, the common but mistaken assumption that time in solitude necessarily leads to loneliness and isolation may be explained by third variables, such as living alone, being widowed, having no (surviving) children, or worsening health <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Grenade & Boldy, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Previous research has showed that people increasingly gain more control over their time alone as they get older (Larson, 1990) but the planning that goes into how that time is spent is less understood.
text.formatted: Previous research has showed that people increasingly gain more control over their time alone as they get older <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Larson, 1990)</ref> but the planning that goes into how that time is spent is less understood.

text.text: Literature around older adult's decision making and planning when approaching retirement often focuses on how a person assesses their financial situation before deciding to retire (Ramli et al., 2023), and Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB; Ajzen, 1991) has received considerable empirical attention in this area (Ingale & Paluri, 2025).
text.formatted: Literature around older adult's decision making and planning when approaching retirement often focuses on how a person assesses their financial situation before deciding to retire <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(Ramli et al., 2023)</ref>, and Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB; <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Ajzen, 1991)</ref> has received considerable empirical attention in this area <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Ingale & Paluri, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The theory posits that the intention to carry out a behavior is shaped by three main factors: an individual's personal evaluations of the behavior (personal attitude), the degree to which significant others approve of or value it (subjective norms), and the individual's confidence in being able to carry it out (perceived control).

Research supporting TPB has showed that older adult's intention to retire is sharpened not only by their own attitudes (Kim et al., 2025), but also pressures from people around them (Nguyen et al., 2026), and availability of savings to pension coverage that allow financial security after retirement (Kim et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Research supporting TPB has showed that older adult's intention to retire is sharpened not only by their own attitudes <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Kim et al., 2025)</ref>, but also pressures from people around them <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Nguyen et al., 2026)</ref>, and availability of savings to pension coverage that allow financial security after retirement <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Kim et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In the present study, we do not use TPB to examine whether solitude shapes people's intentions to retire.
Instead, we apply its three components to a different domain within the transition: time spent alone.
Distinguishing solitude from loneliness and isolation makes this possible.

Here, solitude refers broadly to time spent alone during retirement, recognizing that such time may be experienced positively but may also become associated with loneliness and isolation depending on life circumstances and available social opportunities.

We conducted qualitative interviews with questions built around the TPB framework (Ajzen, 1991) to understand how older adults anticipate and plan for their time alone after they retire and how they expect to cope with its abundance.
text.formatted: We conducted qualitative interviews with questions built around the TPB framework <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Ajzen, 1991)</ref> to understand how older adults anticipate and plan for their time alone after they retire and how they expect to cope with its abundance.

text.text: Applied to retirement and solitude, this framework suggests that how retirees use and respond to alone time would depend on: 1.
Attitudes: whether they see solitude as beneficial, neutral, or undesirable; 2.
Subjective norms: whether people in their lives -such as family, friends, or carers -approve of or value solitude; and 3.
Perceived control: their confidence in managing and using that time in ways that suit their preferences.

Rather than testing TPB as a predictive model, we use these components -attitudes, subjective norms, and perceived control -as a lens for exploring how people who have retired or plan to retire anticipate, plan for, and experience time alone, a domain that has received little attention in the retirement transition literature.
Previous research has shown that people may hold different attitudes toward solitude.
Some see it as beneficial for rest, self-reflection, and creativity, while others associate it with exclusion or social rejection (Nguyen et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Some see it as beneficial for rest, self-reflection, and creativity, while others associate it with exclusion or social rejection <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Nguyen et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: When solitude is seen as a choice, it can help regulate high-arousal emotions (Nguyen et al., 2018), foster calmness and relaxation (Rodriguez et al., 2025), encourage creativity and self-reflection (Long & Averill, 2003), and promote freedom and autonomy (Weinstein et al., 2023).
text.formatted: When solitude is seen as a choice, it can help regulate high-arousal emotions <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Nguyen et al., 2018)</ref>, foster calmness and relaxation <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Rodriguez et al., 2025)</ref>, encourage creativity and self-reflection <ref type="bibr">(Long & Averill, 2003)</ref>, and promote freedom and autonomy <ref type="bibr">(Weinstein et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, when individuals associate solitude with loneliness or experience episodes of solitude as imposed rather than chosen (Rodriguez et al., 2025), it can bring negative affect, rumination, and declines in mental health (Lay et al., 2019).
text.formatted: In contrast, when individuals associate solitude with loneliness or experience episodes of solitude as imposed rather than chosen <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Rodriguez et al., 2025)</ref>, it can bring negative affect, rumination, and declines in mental health <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Lay et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: For retirees, viewing time alone as an opportunity to unwind or reflect, rather than as unwanted isolation, may be particularly important for well-being.
Even when older adults find solitude restorative, carers or family members may interpret it as loneliness, and believe that one needs company and help at old ages (Ost-Mor et al., 2021).

text.text: In these situations, individuals may genuinely experience time alone as positive and empowering, yet others' reactions can undermine that experience, making them feel selfconscious and adding a layer of stigma that makes solitude harder to enjoy.
Beyond attitudes and others' judgments, retirees also face the question of how to fill the time that was once occupied by work tasks and responsibilities.
How they spend this time can shape their adjustment to retirement.
Many older adults have more control over their daily schedules than younger people (Larson, 1990), and retirement may further enhance this autonomy.
text.formatted: Many older adults have more control over their daily schedules than younger people <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Larson, 1990)</ref>, and retirement may further enhance this autonomy.

text.text: This freedom may help them tolerate solitude better than their younger counterparts.

Engaging in hobbies, maintaining routines, staying physically active (Beck et al., 2010), or taking up new interests (Ross & Drentea, 1998) can help preserve a sense of control and reduce the risk of loneliness.

text.text: However, not everyone finds this transition easy; some retirees struggle to establish new routines (Ross & Drentea, 1998), and the reduced structure compared to working life can make the adjustment challenging.

text.text: By exploring how older adults anticipate and experience time spent alone after retirement, this research aims to understand how retirees navigate solitude in the context of expanded discretionary time, shifting social roles, and evolving identity.

Drawing on the TPB, we focus specifically on retirees' attitudes toward solitude, perceived social norms surrounding time spent alone, and their sense of control over how that time is structured and experienced.
In particular, we ask: RQ1.
How do retirees perceive solitude -positively or negatively -and how does this perception shape their experience?
RQ2.
How do people in retirees' lives influence their engagement with alone time?
How do retirees manage and use their time alone effectively?

In addressing these questions, we seek to provide a nuanced understanding of the retirementsolitude relationship, highlighting both benefits and challenges, and identifying insights that may inform supportive interventions and policies for aging populations

text.text: Because the qualitative interviews contain personal content, full interview transcripts are not publicly shared to protect participant confidentiality.
Transcripts may be made available upon request to the corresponding author.
We advertised the study widely across multiple channels.
Particularly, we recruited from university's community through institutional newsletters and workshops for university staff who was preparing to retire.
We also distributed flyers to the local council, local non-profit organisations and venues, and posted them on various social media platforms.
Participants who contacted us were asked to book an individual or focus group interview through an online calendar hosted on Calendly (2025).
text.formatted: Participants who contacted us were asked to book an individual or focus group interview through an online calendar hosted on <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Calendly (2025)</ref>.

text.text: Interviews were conducted between February and April of 2023.
This study was approved by the We recruited participants who were planning to retire or who had retired recently.
The goal was to capture how participants anticipate spending time alone as they think about retirement, as well as how the transition unfolds during the first few months after retiring.
Perspectives from those planning to retire reflect more anticipatory attitudes and preconceptions, whereas those who had already retired reflect current experiences and challenges.
Because the study explored both individuals' personal experiences of solitude and the social norms surrounding it, we combined individual interviews and focus groups.

One-on-one interviews allowed participants to share personal experiences in depth, whereas focus groups allowed participants to respond to and reflect on others' perspectives (Lambert & Loiselle, 2008).
text.formatted: One-on-one interviews allowed participants to share personal experiences in depth, whereas focus groups allowed participants to respond to and reflect on others' perspectives <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Lambert & Loiselle, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Our goal was not to compare interview and focus group data systematically, but to enrich the dataset through both individual reflection and interactive discussion.
In total, we conducted 19 individual interviews and two focus groups (a group of two and a group of three).
Prior to interviews, participants filled out a questionnaire to report their demographics.
Interviews were conducted in English and lasted for one hour to one and a half hour.
Online interviews were conducted and recorded via Microsoft Teams (2025), and in-person interviews were recorded using Dictaphones.

Several measures were in place to ensure confidentiality; all participants were asked to not share personal information during the interview, with focus group participants using anonymous ID to refer to one another.
Two researchers carried out focus group with one asking questions and one taking notes.
At the beginning of each session, we asked the participant to confirm was planning to retire or retired.
Specifically, the interviewer told the participants: "For this project, we are interviewing people who are going through life transitions about their thoughts and experiences with solitude.
By solitude, I mean times when you are not interacting with someone else in person, not talking on the phone or chatting with other people online."
After each interview participants were debriefed, and interviewers completed reflexivity statements, documenting prior assumptions about the participant and reflections on the interview interaction.
The survey was administered prior to the interview and included questions about age, gender, ethnicity, employment status, level of education, marital status, residence and living status.

Participants reported their current physical health (EVS/WVS, 2021), the average number of hours they spend alone daily (Nguyen et al., 2023), subjective amount of time spent in solitude (Coplan et al., 2019), life satisfaction (EVS/WVS, 2021), and listed activities that they engage in when alone.

text.text: Interview questions were initially developed based on the TPB to capture participants' attitudes toward solitude, perceived social norms surrounding time spent alone, and their perceived behavioral control over how that time is structured.
The questions were then refined based on feedback from two expert focus groups consisting of four solitude researchers.
The purpose of these groups was to ensure the interview questions would meaningfully capture participants' intentions toward time spent alone after the experts were provided the TPB framework.
The final set of semistructured questions aimed to capture participants' perceptions of solitude, which was defined as both a physical and subjective experience (Larson, 1990; Long et al., 2003).
text.formatted: The final set of semistructured questions aimed to capture participants' perceptions of solitude, which was defined as both a physical and subjective experience <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Larson, 1990;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Long et al., 2003)</ref>.

text.text: There were ten open-ended questions about their general attitudes toward solitude, the influence of their social environment on their alone time, and their perceived control over how they manage solitude during retirement.
The interview guide is presented in Supplementary materials (see Appendix S1).
Online interview video and in-person interview audio were transcribed by the research team.
Interview recordings were transcribed non-verbatim as outlined in (McLellan et al., 2003).
text.formatted: Interview recordings were transcribed non-verbatim as outlined in <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(McLellan et al., 2003)</ref>.

text.text: One transcript per participant was produced, including for those who were part of focus groups.
Interview transcribers also completed brief reflexivity notes during transcription to document reflections on the interview and initial ideas about potential themes.
They were asked to flag responses that appeared unusually generic or difficult to interpret so that the principal investigator could review the recordings for data quality.
Reflexive thematic analysis, as outlined by Braun and Clarke (2006, 2012), was employed to analyse the interview transcripts and generate key themes related to retirement and solitude.
text.formatted: Reflexive thematic analysis, as outlined by <ref type="bibr">Braun and</ref> <ref type="bibr">Clarke (2006, 2012)</ref>, was employed to analyse the interview transcripts and generate key themes related to retirement and solitude.

text.text: Our analysis adopted a primarily semantic and realist orientation, focusing on participants' descriptions of their experiences and the meanings they attributed to them.
Rather than emphasizing frequency counts, the analysis aimed to identify recurring patterns as well as points of divergence across participants' narratives.

The analytic approach combined both inductive and deductive processes; while themes were primarily developed inductively from the data, the interpretations were informed by the Theory of Planned Behavior, with a focus on how participants' narratives reflected their personal attitudes, subjective norms, and perceived behavioural control around time alone after retirement.
The analysis followed Braun and Clarke's six-phase approach.
First, seven researchers (DK, PT, PJC, GC, ZG, ZH, MX) independently familiarized themselves with the data by reading and rereading the transcripts and noted down initial observations.
In the second phase, they generated initial codes, which were iteratively reviewed and refined through discussions with the senior researcher on the team (TVN).
These codes were then organized into potential themes in phase three, with themes being reviewed and refined in phase four to ensure coherence and consistency across the dataset.
In phase five, the themes were condensed, defined and named, with the lead researcher (BY) who did not participate in the previous phases finalizing the thematic structure.
The lead and senior researchers then reviewed the final set of themes and continued to refine them in response to feedback from the editor and reviewers, reducing overlap among themes.
Throughout the process, the research team maintained ongoing discussions to refine interpretations of themes and codes.
Data analysis was facilitated using Dedoose software (2025).
The interview protocol and interview questions were developed by TVN.
PT and DK conducted the expert focus groups, through which solitude researchers provided feedback on the interview protocol prior to data collection.
Interviews were conducted by trained members of the research team (AK, IQ, JW, MX, ZH, PT, and DK), with PT and DK also facilitating the participant focus groups.
All interviewers received training in the interview procedure and were also trained to write reflexivity statements before conducting interviews.
The same team members who conducted interviews also transcribed the recordings.
The team's positionality shaped this division of roles during the analysis phases.
Our axiological position was that solitude is a neutral experience, neither inherently positive nor negative, whose meaning depends on the person and context.
The last author and senior researcher (TVN) studies solitude from this perspective but is also familiar with research on solitude in older adulthood that tends to emphasize its benefits.
To reduce the risk of this knowledge shaping how the data were coded, TVN did not generate codes; she joined the analysis once initial codes had been developed to help identify and interpret themes.
The coders were undergraduate research assistants who had basic knowledge of solitude and were trained both in thematic analysis and in the team's view of solitude as a neutral experience.

BY, an experienced qualitative researcher with limited prior familiarity with the solitude literature, offered an interpretive lens grounded in participants' lived experiences rather than the focal theoretical framework (TPB).
None of the team members were retired or approaching retirement at the time of the study, and all were younger than the participants.
We therefore approached older adulthood and retirement as outsiders, relying on participants' accounts rather than personal experience.
While our analysis focused on participants' own descriptions of their experiences, we recognize that the themes reflect the team's interpretation of those accounts.
The sample consisted of 23 participants aged 58 to 66 years, most of whom were around the typical retirement age.

There were 16 men (69.6%) and seven women (30.4%), and all were born and residing in the United Kingdom; our participants were recruited from local areas, including Newcastle, Sunderland, Darlington, and Durham 2 .

The sample was ethnically diverse, with seven participants (30.4%) identifying as English, Welsh, Scottish, Northern Irish, or British; seven (30.4%) as having another Black, Black British, or Caribbean background; four (17.4%) as having another Mixed or multiple ethnic background; three (13.0%) as Caribbean; one (4.3%) as African; and one (4.3%) as White and Black African.
Most participants were married (82.6%) and everyone was living with others in their household.
All of our participants reported good or very good physical health.
Fifteen participants (65.2%) were already retired, and eight (34.8%) were planning to retire within the following year.

Among those retired, 13 had retired within the 3 months before the interviews, consistent with our inclusion criteria; two participants who had been retired longer (8 months and 2 years) were also included.
All participants except one had either associate, undergraduate or postgraduate degrees.

text.text: When asked about their everyday experiences of solitude, participants reported spending between one and eight hours alone during a typical waking day.
Most participants said that the amount of alone time they currently experienced was "about right."
A summary of the types of activities participants typically engage in when alone is presented in the Supplementary Materials (see Figure S1).
text.formatted: A summary of the types of activities participants typically engage in when alone is presented in the Supplementary Materials (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">S1</ref>).

text.text: These responses suggest that time spent alone was often structured around personally meaningful, leisure, routine activities, or rest and relaxation.
In the interviews, participants discussed their experiences of or anticipation of retirement in general, while offering unique insights around their perceptions of their time alone.

Three themes were developed: (1) retirement requires renegotiating boundaries and routines to make space for both social contacts and solitude, (2) newfound solitude offers retirees both opportunities and risks, and (3) retirees may face several obstacles in adjusting to life after retirement (see Table 1).

text.text: Themes and sub-themes are presented with selected excerpts below; additional excerpts for each sub-theme are available on OSF.
Table 1.
Themes, Sub-themes, and Key Ideas in Participants' Accounts of Solitude During the Transition to Retirement 1.
Retirement requires renegotiating boundaries and routines to make space for both social contacts and solitude 1.1.

Retirees embrace newfound freedom after retirement and renegotiate boundaries with co-workers, family, and friends to protect their time • Greater autonomy and freedom • Redefined work-life boundaries • Carve out alone time within family life • Face challenge in getting family members to recognize one's need for personal time • Family members adapting over time to respect and support solitude 1.2.

Losing the structure of work leaves retirees needing new routines to manage unstructured time alone • Major shift in daily routine and loss of structure • More unstructured time and more time alone • Daily routines and structure help with adjustment • Pet companionship helps with structure and reduces loneliness 1.3.

Retirees proactively seek new social connections, ways to give back, to offset the social loss retirement brings • Reduced social interactions previously provided through work, leaving everyday interactions limited to immediate family members • Expressed need to interact more with people and expand social networks through extracurricular activities (clubs/groups/community activities) • Seeking mentorship or volunteer opportunities to give back and build purpose 2.
Newfound solitude offers retirees both opportunities 2.1.

Solitude gives retirees uninterrupted time to reflect, be authentic, and pursue selfimproving activities • Reflect on identity, decisions, and life direction • Be oneself, free from social judgment • Pursue fitness and health-maintaining and risks activities • Explore personal projects and hobbies 2.2.

Unstructured or excessive solitude can heighten rumination, disconnection, and loss of social confidence • Difficulty filling time meaningfully, and the isolation that comes with it • Having too much time on your own might turn thoughts inward in unwelcome ways 3.
Retirees may face several obstacles in adjusting to life after retirement 3.1.

Financial security (or its absence) shapes retirees' ability to plan for and enjoy retirement without worry • Healthcare costs and reduced income create financial uncertainty • Limited financial resources restrict travel, hobbies, meaningful activities 3.2.

Health limitations constrain activity and increase isolation • Poor health and reduced mobility limit participation activities, raising the risk of loneliness and boredom • Illness and physical pain can make time alone in retirement difficult The transition out of work was most clearly reflected in changes to daily routine, with a large part of the day no longer spent working.
For one participant who has retired, this was a welcome change, offering a sense of freedom or autonomy.
Another participant who is planning to retire anticipates that they will have more control over their own schedule, which might provide new opportunities to enjoy life and focus on self-care.
"What I like about it [retirement] is having the ability to make decisions for yourself and not be... constrained to meeting deadlines and class times or any of those deadlines associated with work."

(ID: 91; 63 years old, planning to retire in 1 year) This anticipated freedom extended beyond simply having more time -for those approaching retirement, it also meant finally having the opportunity to pursue activities that they did not have time for when they were still working.

Notably, participant #91 defined freedom by what they were free from -time constraints imposed by others such as deadlines and class schedules; as such, retirement marks the beginning of reclaiming ownership of time itself, as their day became more flexible and less constrained by social demands and other people's schedule.
However, this freed-up time does not automatically happen without obstruction.
Retirees also had to renegotiate boundaries with former colleagues, since past work identity was also tied to the people with whom participants interacted with at work.

This topic around interactions with previous co-workers came up in one focus group where two participants (51 & 52) shared their experiences of navigating these boundaries with former work colleagues.
text.formatted: This topic around interactions with previous co-workers came up in one focus group where two participants (51 & 52) shared their experiences of navigating these boundaries with former work colleagues.

text.text: Both participants expressed that it was important to distance themselves, with different levels of success.
This helped them maintain a sense of separation and peace away from work-related conversations in the transition to and following retirement.
This separation was more difficult for participant #51 who continued socializing with their former colleagues.
This suggests that for some retirees, retirement is not just about stopping to show up at work one day but an ongoing process of negotiating boundaries with those who are still tied to work.
Continued interactions with former colleagues might cause frustration if the colleagues continue to expect being able to talk about work stresses like before.
"Some of me colleagues at work still offload… cause they're still working, they think oh you know, have a chat [name], have a chat with me about it.
But sometimes it's just, I don't want to know, it's not part of my life anymore, working.
And I don't, I don't really want to go sit and talk to people about work, about all their problems."
(ID: 51; 59 years old, retired 2 years ago)
Beyond renegotiating boundaries with former colleagues, retirees also had to negotiate them at home.
The transition to being home more often could bring changes to social dynamics with those they lived with.
Family members, particularly spouses and children, often needed to adjust to the retiree's increased presence at home, which could occasionally lead to disruptions in their time alone.
Even so, participants saw protecting some time for themselves as important to their quality of life.
This need for balance was not always easy to assert.
The desire for time alone after retirement can come with guilt, as one participant who had been retired the longest in our study expressed that they felt selfish for wanting that.
"Family obligations, they think you've got all the time to sort of focus on them, when this is my time.
I've done stuff for you, and this is my time to not have to run around after everybody.
I think that's quite hard for people.

And friends, they seem to want…I've got a friend who, she does not work, so she thinks, it's okay if me spend a lot of time with her but when I really want to be on my own, that sounds so selfish…" (ID: 51; 59 years old, retired 2 years ago)
In some cases, retirees found it difficult to express a need for alone time, as they did not want to hurt others' feelings.
Rather than stating it directly, some participants expressed their need for solitude subtly through showing the importance of this time to them so other family members could understand.

"My wife was having a little bit of a problem with the amount of time I'm spending alone, but later on when she started to witness the transformation, the confidence I was gaining, the things I was learning and she realized that it was kind of like beneficial."

(ID: 26; 60 years old, retired 2 months ago) Over time, this could develop into a mutual understanding between them and their family when personal time was needed, and they had a dedicated space in the home where they could focus on themselves without interruptions.
"I have a room that used to be my home office where I used to work from home.
So, when I enter that room, it's automatic.
Nobody comes to disrupt me until I come out of there again, like they used to do when I worked.
If I enter that room, they know our father is having some alone time."
(ID: 61; 61 years old, retired 2 months ago)
Eventually, many participants noted that their families had come to respect their need for solitude, treating it as something to be expected rather than questioned.

Taken together, these accounts mean that retirement did not just automatically give participants more solitude; retirement removed the structure that going to work previously provided, along with a socially accepted reason to be unavailable to others.
When such structure was gone, even after retirement, our participants continued having to negotiate, protect and justify autonomy and ownership over their time.
The loss of structure may also present some other challenges.
One participant, thinking about their upcoming retirement, expressed mixed feelings and shared in the interview that they were very worried about having more time by themselves than before.
"I think this will be time for me to rest since I be under any pressure at work.
Ah that's an advantage, but then as a disadvantage, the switch from the work setup to mostly staying at home and hanging out just by myself."

(ID: 25; 59 years old, planning to retire in 3 months) For some of our participants, it can be difficult to adapt to the routine of less work and more alone time, especially at the start of retirement.
Several participants described the challenge of adjusting to a daily routine that was no longer structured around work schedules.
"Most people like routine...my background as I said was in the [previous field of work], so one learns to know what time it is and to appreciate and run your schedule due to time...
I am quite time oriented.
And so that will be a challenge for me, not to have those constraints or chains on me about time management and that freedom will in itself bring challenges."
(ID: 91; 63 years old, planning to retire in 1 year)
One retiree described needing to balance the appeal of having more time alone with everyday routines and obligations that structure daily life.
"The transition wasn't really that easy because you know I had a lot of time at hand and having seen the benefit of solitude, it was kind of was tempting to have more time to myself.
But, as I told you, there is this normal life as somebody has to maintain even when I'm having time alone, you can't just have a whole day out alone.
You know the other things you have to… you have to go shopping, you have to do basically there's a lot of things that have to be done."
(ID: 61; 61 years old, retired 2 months ago)
For another participant, their daily routines were part of their pre-retirement identity.
This participant was a caretaker for their now-deceased parents, so they found themselves spending a lot of time alone because their child was also away for college.
When retirement happened suddenly like this case, it could feel like a loss of identity.
Similarly, retirement may result in fewer opportunities for social interaction, and this could lead to loneliness.
Even for someone who hasn't retired, this can be a concern, especially if they have spent their life prior to retirement being around other people.
Given the loss of the normal routines of coming to work every day, many retirees acknowledged it was important to build in new structure for their solitude after retirement.
This included getting ready in the morning, doing house chores and shopping, or having general goals for the day.
For retirees, keeping busy by planning activities, social time, and alone time can improve experiences of retirement.

This highlights not only the role of daily routine in maintaining a sense of safety and control for older adults (Li et al., 2023; Klinedinst et al., 2022), but also the importance of being able to adapt and stay active after retirement (Karlsson et al., 2025).
text.formatted: This highlights not only the role of daily routine in maintaining a sense of safety and control for older adults <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Li et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Klinedinst et al., 2022)</ref>, but also the importance of being able to adapt and stay active after retirement <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Karlsson et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, while the loss of routine might initially cause distress, the ability to embrace that change to regain structure of daily life after leaving work helps older adults improve their retirement experience.
"It was hard the first two months.
But now I've adjusted to it so it's somehow normal...
I made it a habit, a routine.
Something that I do every day.
Like when I wake up, I take my breakfast do some gardening stuff, lunch, watch some movies or read some books then I go to sleep.
So its habit.
I do it every day."

(ID: 16; 65 years old, retired 3 months ago) Most importantly, reflected in the quote below and also the next sub-theme is the significance of continuing interactions with other people daily, which is consistent with the positive effect of having routine social interactions on older adults' affective well-being (Luo et al., 2024).

text.text: "Make plans to be with people and have a plan for your day, even if you are by yourself.
Don't just get up and take each hour.
Make a start.

Have a start for that day where you know you'll get set times and set…things to do in a certain length of time…and yeah, and just tryin'… enjoy and tryin' find some hobbies…and some interests that you enjoy doing…you know go backpacking."
(ID: 09; 62 years old, retired 8 months ago)
In that sense, having a pet provides that stable companionship.
Pets were seen as an important source of emotional support and connection during retirement.
Beyond simply offering company, pets played a role in fostering social interactions with other pet owners and promoting a sense of routine in daily life.
The presence of pets provided structure through consistent responsibilities, such as feeding schedules or daily walks.
These activities not only helped maintain a sense of purpose but also offered regular opportunities to stay active and get outside, which was beneficial for physical and mental well-being.
Because retirees may let go of past social relationships at work, this led to a reduction in daily socialization.
Particularly for those whose children were not around and those who were more sociable, no longer going to work led to a lot more time spent alone at home, which could be challenging.
"I usually socialize a lot, uh while like I was at work.

But, when I go to retired, the issue of socializing, it's kind of reduced…So, I'm just alone at home, whenever during, mostly it is during the day and, this is kind of a challenge to me, because you see, I'm a social, more social guy and I need, I usually talk frequently and I need somebody to talk to."
(ID: 15; 60 years old, retired 1 month ago) At the same time, opportunities to meet people and build new relationships organically may be limited.
For some participants, social contact after retirement was largely confined to immediate family members, which sometimes felt insufficient.
Interacting with others outside established relationships was described as an important source of enrichment and something that retirees aimed for after retirement.
As such, anticipating their retirement in a year, one participant expressed trying to actively seek out new social connections.
"Some of the negatives I can see how…it would become very easy to become over isolated.
If I'm by myself a lot.
So, I think I would have to make effort to make myself go out and...create a new social life for myself.
Perhaps join some groups."
(ID: 50; 63 years old, planning to retire in 1 year)
Participants emphasized the importance of balancing time spent alone with time spent with others during retirement.
While finding this balance could initially be challenging, many reported that it became easier with time.
Fitting in social activities could also be part of establishing daily structure that -as mentioned in the previous sub-theme -was much needed after retirement.
Many retirees discussed planning social activities, joining clubs, and regularly attending groups to alleviate negative experiences in solitude.
These social moments also helped retirees to foster and maintain social connections.

For some, seeking new social connections is also coupled with pursuing activities that give them meaning, through volunteering, mentoring to share knowledge, or offering support to those within their community.
They saw this not only as a way to expand their social networks but also as an opportunity to give back.
"Give yourself time to help others because lots of people have helped me in the past so it's nice to give things back if you can."

(ID: 34; 58 years old, retired 2 months ago) These accounts suggest that, for many participants, retirement marked a new chapter in which to build social connections -an indicator of positive ageing (Menkin et al., 2017).
text.formatted: (ID: 34; 58 years old, retired 2 months ago) These accounts suggest that, for many participants, retirement marked a new chapter in which to build social connections -an indicator of positive ageing <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Menkin et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast to the common narrative of old age as a time of cutting back on social relationships, many participants planned to take up activities that would allow them to meet new people.

Yet this was not simply about expanding their social circles; their desire for connection appeared intentional and purposeful, tied to spaces and activities that retirees valued and that gave their lives meaning.

Taken together, our findings suggest that while retirement may mean letting go of connections built through workplace or other social obligations, it also opens up opportunities to form new relationships that better fit one's psychological needs.

Theme 2: Newfound solitude offers retirees both opportunities and risks Sub-theme 2.1: Solitude gives retirees uninterrupted time to reflect, be authentic, and pursue self-improving activities During retirement, solitude time can serve a wide range of purposes, including staying active, keeping busy, exploring interests, relaxing, being authentic and reflecting.

Complementing the previous theme that suggests life after retirement meant reclaim ownership over one's time, many of our participants expressed interests in self-improvement activities, reflecting a positive outlook toward aging.
First and foremost, finding more time for physical activities was a common theme.

"[Location where the participant lives] has the countryside so just cycling and walking like today once I come from here I will go home and go for a walk for an hour, don't know if I mentioned that but every other day in the morning I'm walking for at least an hour trying to get my 10,000 steps in."
(ID: 34; 58 years old, retired 2 months ago) This time is often viewed as an opportunity to engage in different activities, learn new skills, and explore or revisit hobbies.
For some retirees, it meant finally having the time to reconnect with past interests they had previously set aside, such as crafting, electronics, or outdoor activities.
Others saw it as a chance to try new pursuits they had been curious about but never had the time for.
"I may choose to spend more time pursuing hobbies, or things that I didn't have time for while working."
(ID: 72; 59 years old, planning to retire in 1 month) Retirement also provided participants the freedom to focus on personal projects.
For retirees this can involve applying the skills developed during their working life, but now they had the autonomy to pursue them purely for personal interest rather than professional obligation.
Alongside these active pursuits, solitude was also valued as a time to slow down.
Solitude was frequently used to restore energy and relax.
Retirees valued the opportunity to rest and rejuvenate, often engaging in low-profile or calming activities to enjoy peace and quiet.
This period of rest was considered important, especially after years of work-related stress and busyness.
"After I retired I needed to have a lot of time relaxing because I've been working for all over 30 years so when I'm able to reflect my life.
I think it's positive because I need to also have my time to think and also relax."
(ID: 24; 60 years old, retired 2 months ago) Even the participant that was worried about their retirement anticipated using this time for rest.
For those who have retired, this increased sense of restfulness was because they no longer had to think about work.
They were able to enjoy time alone for what it is without having to worry about what would happen the next day.
Beyond rest, participants mentioned how spending time alone has also improved their psychological health, with a few describing enhanced self-focus, a sense of authenticity, and selfawareness.
Solitude allowed retirees the freedom to prioritize their own desires and engage in activities without feeling obligated to meet others' needs or expectations.
This shift enabled them to prioritize personal well-being after years of balancing work-life responsibilities.
Time spent in solitude was often described as an opportunity to be authentic, free from social judgements or pressure from others.
For those in retirement, solitude may offer time to connect with one's authentic self without the need to perform or conform to social expectations.
"I feel like it's the real me when I'm on my own...
So, I feel utterly comfortable...
Yes.
At peace with myself, comfortable.
I don't feel I am... having to put on a face, a public face.
The relaxation of it...and I'm comfortable."
(ID: 50; 63 years old, planning to retire in 1 year) This freedom from others' expectations also created room for self-reflection.
For both retirees and those who are planning to retire, solitude can also be an opportunity to reflect on life, relationships, and personal experiences.
This reflection can lead to self-development and exploration, providing higher levels of self-awareness.
During retirement, alone time can be important for thinking critically with the aim to further develop, connect and understand the self.
"I reflect on my life, how, how I want to plan my life.
The best things I want to do for myself during that [solitude] time.
I do reflect about the past, how things have been, where I went wrong and where I want to change things."

(ID: 78; 61 years old, retired 1 month ago) Reflection was not only about correcting past mistakes; for some, it was also a way to focus on the positive, on their own happiness, and on the things that they enjoy doing.

While a few accounts mentioned in previous themes suggest that retirement is the time that people want to build new connections and to give back to society, one retiree recognized that this was also the time to do things for themselves, as they have spent a large portion of their earlier life doing things for others.
As such, retirement can also be an opportunity to gain better understanding of oneself.

Overall, this theme suggests that retirement freed up space for a kind of self-compassion, giving participants permission to prioritize their own needs after years of meeting the demands of work and others.

Consistent with research on the benefits of solitude for self-reflection (Ost-Mor et al., 2021; Thomas, 2023; Weinstein et al., 2023), participants' positive attitudes toward time alone may help them draw greater benefit from it.
text.formatted: Consistent with research on the benefits of solitude for self-reflection <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Ost-Mor et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Thomas, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Weinstein et al., 2023)</ref>, participants' positive attitudes toward time alone may help them draw greater benefit from it.

text.text: Through reflection, participants were able to identify what mattered to them and direct their time toward enjoyable activities, personal interests, and their own happiness.
In contrast, solitude in retirement is not without its challenges.
Spending time alone can be a difficult experience due to a reduction in social contact or restrictions in choices of enjoyable activities available in solitude due to poor health.
Prolonged negative experiences of solitude in retirement can be particularly difficult.
Particularly, being alone can sometimes put people at risk of negative and persistent thoughts about themselves and their life.
For retirees, negative thoughts might relate to regrets about retirement, worries about what to do with their time in retirement, worries about social isolation and comparison to peers.
Some of these thoughts can be existential, as noted in the quote below.

"During the solitude time you must be stressed, remember, unless you are not a human, because sometimes you think things outside the box and you start thinking, how will this life be after maybe after death?
What's next, what happens?
So maybe I can say that's what happens in that time."
(ID: 55; 60 years old, retired 1 month ago)
Time in solitude can amplify retirees' relational disconnection from others due to being more physically removed from their old community.
Some retirees disclosed experiences of negative mood when having too much alone time.
For those who desire to interact with others and engage with the community, solitude can be particularly isolating.
Some retirees were worried their social skills might decline if they did not maintain the same levels of interactions that they were used to have preretirement.
"This downside of being in solitude in that when I'm alone for too long, it can be easy to feel isolated or disconnected from others.
So and again, being disconnected from other you know can create room for the pressure or stress which can lead to some mental health.
So that's the major disadvantage I on, on my part I think."

(ID: 88; 60 years old, retired 1 month ago) Compounded by both the increase in alone time and the transition away from work, solitude can sometimes bring about feelings of being "lost" or not using this time to its 'fullest'.
For some retirees, this meant not wanting to 'slow down' or 'do nothing' when in solitude.
For others, it became important to use solitude time to 'achieve something'.
Experiencing boredom was a common theme when retirees talked about spending time alone.
In retirement, boredom often arises from not feeling as though there are any activities to do or feeling restricted in how time alone can be spent, which could be overwhelming.
One particular participant spoke about this risk of "sitting on a chair and doing nothing".
For this person, this time of not having something to do could spiral into negative thoughts and even destructive habits.
"If you on your own for too long, then you tend to dwell on things that really shouldn't be at the forefront of your mind.
And I think some people can't cope with that…and they turn to drink.
And then they feel so bad in the morning.
Then they go, you know, I'll go and have a cup of coffee, make yourself feel better.
And they had a, you know, a glass of Brandy to get themselves going.
And that becomes a vicious cycle."
(ID: 82; 65 years old, planning to retire in 10 months) Overall, while solitude in retirement offered opportunities for personal growth and reflection, it also carried psychological risks.
Without a clear sense of purpose or adequate social engagement, some retirees felt vulnerable to feelings of loneliness, boredom, and existential doubt.
Notably, the participants who described these risks were often the same ones who had described its benefits in the previous sub-theme.
This suggests that the positive and negative aspects of solitude do not simply reflect individual differences, with some retirees benefiting from time alone and others struggling with it.
Rather, the same person could experience both, indicating that participants held a nuanced view of what solitude can offer and when it might become harmful.

Theme 3: Retirees may face several obstacles in adjusting to life after retirement Sub-theme 3.1: Financial security (or its absence) shapes retirees' ability to plan for and enjoy retirement without worry Finally, after having reflected on all the positives and negatives that might come with retirement and the increased time for solitude, our participants identified a few obstacles that might prevent them from fully embracing their retirement.
For both those approaching retirement and those already retired, financial stability was a prominent priority.
The transition from a salary to a fixed or reduced income raised worries about maintaining pre-retirement lifestyles.

"So it fills me worried because sometimes the things that I used to do are usually things erm when I sit down and have...that my solitude may develop some fear because I'm going to miss some bit of achievement or some bit of things, free time the way I used to spend my life so I'm able to fear because I'm not on that monthly payroll that I used to be so it may develop some form of anxiety."

(ID: 24; 60 years old, retired 2 months ago) Beyond being able to afford what they had while earning a salary, participants recognized that financial security was essential to enjoying retirement more broadly.
Retirees wanted the means to engage in meaningful activities, many of which involved a financial cost.

Having access to other sources of income outside of full-time work (such as taking on a part-time job), having savings and adequate pensions, was seen as fundamental to maintaining a good quality of life in retirement.

"I think that's a big factor in how people cope with the retirement because…if you have the savings or the income to travel and go and holiday with friends or your family, then that's certainly gonna add enjoyment to your life, but there must be a lot of people that retired that don't have that the resources to do that."
(ID: 09; 62 years old, retired 8 months ago) This theme reinforces previous research showing that financial security is a key consideration when people plan for retirement (Nguyen et al., 2026).
text.formatted: (ID: 09; 62 years old, retired 8 months ago) This theme reinforces previous research showing that financial security is a key consideration when people plan for retirement <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Nguyen et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Our findings extend this work by suggesting that financial security is not only about maintaining an existing lifestyle, but also about enabling new pursuits that make life after retirement more rewarding and meaningful.
Health was also an important factor influencing retirees' experiences of loneliness.
Participants noted that poor physical or mental health could limit their ability to enjoy retirement and to use alone time in ways that felt positive.
Health challenges could make it harder to maintain an active lifestyle, participate in social groups, or find variety in daily routines -factors that might otherwise reduce boredom or isolation.

"If you don't have your health when you're retired, then…I'm not saying that that would equate to loneliness, but there's a probably a higher risk that you've been more lonelier if your health is poor...
So there are probably lots of people that would normally maybe join activities, join groups that they can't do that because of their health."
(ID: 09; 62 years old, retired 8 months ago)
Pain and declining health due to old age also makes it difficult to focus.
One participant mentioned that being sick interfered with their ability to reflect on their life.
"What makes it difficult is when perhaps when you are sick because you may feel unwell and according with our age maybe our immunity is usually weak.
Because I'm also a diabetic person so I think that me too when I am sick I don't have a full time to reflect that I need to reflect on my life so it's usually a bit difficult."
(ID: 24; 60 years old, retired 2 months ago) Taken together, these sub-themes suggest that participants took a pragmatic view of what might stand in the way of a fulfilling retirement.
Rather than pointing to loneliness or a lack of relationships, they identified concrete constraints closely tied to later life: money and health.
Both threaten the autonomy participants valued in retirement, and may determine whether time alone feels like freedom or a constraint.
We mapped the sub-themes identified in this study onto the three components of the TPB, linking each to the component it most closely reflects (Figure 1).
