text.text: Sub-themes describing how participants evaluated their time alone aligned most closely with personal attitudes.

These included embracing newfound freedom and time for solitude, seeing solitude as an opportunity for selfreflection, authenticity, and self-improving activities, and recognizing its risks, such as rumination, disconnection, and loss of social confidence.
Negotiating boundaries with family and former colleagues reflected subjective norms, capturing how others' expectations shaped whether retirees felt able to claim time for themselves.

Finally, building new routines, seeking new spaces and activities for social connection, financial security, and health limitations aligned with perceived behavioral control, as these shaped retirees' capacity to structure and use their time alone in ways that suited them.
Seeking social connection, in particular, reflected intentional effort rather than a general wish for company.

Participants oriented their connections around purposeful and meaningful activities, such as volunteering, mentoring, and community groups, suggesting that they actively shaped not only how much time they spent with others, but also the kind of social engagement that fit their needs.
This qualitative study explored how individuals planning to retire and those who had recently retired anticipate and experience solitude, using the TPB as an organizing lens (Figure 1).
text.formatted: This qualitative study explored how individuals planning to retire and those who had recently retired anticipate and experience solitude, using the TPB as an organizing lens (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1</ref>).

text.text: We discuss our findings in relation to each research question in turn: retirees' attitudes toward solitude (RQ1), the influence of others on their time alone (RQ2), and how they manage and use that time (RQ3).
We then turn to findings from the data that fall outside these questions.
Our first research question asked how retirees perceive solitude and how this perception shapes their experience.

Consistent with the personal attitudes component of the TPB, participants rarely held uniformly positive or negative views; instead, they weighed solitude as both an opportunity and a risk, often within the same person.
The insight we have learned from these interviews is that all of our participants had something meaningful to say about their time alone.

Even those who had not retired showed active deliberation around how they anticipated that time would be, including both challenges as well as benefits, and how they would go about spending that time to optimize their retirement.

For those who had retired, many reported growing appreciation for solitude and greater flexibility in how they spend it, supporting evidence that choice enhances enjoyment (Nguyen et al., 2018; Ost-Mor et al., 2021).
text.formatted: For those who had retired, many reported growing appreciation for solitude and greater flexibility in how they spend it, supporting evidence that choice enhances enjoyment <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Nguyen et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Ost-Mor et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Many retirees also prioritize their autonomy and well-being through activities they pursue in solitude.
Solitude in retirement can be an opportunity for rest and self-reflection, aligning with broader findings on its role in self-regulation (Nguyen et al., 2018; Rodriguez et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Solitude in retirement can be an opportunity for rest and self-reflection, aligning with broader findings on its role in self-regulation <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Nguyen et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Rodriguez et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Many participants described feeling more in tune with themselves when alone, free from social judgment.
This sense of self-connection and privacy was a central part of their solitary experience (Thomas, 2023).
text.formatted: This sense of self-connection and privacy was a central part of their solitary experience <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Thomas, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: However, several participants noted that too much time alone may carry risks, such as boredom, a sense of unfulfillment, and worries about wasting time.

Negative experiences were often tied to feelings of isolation and distress, especially among retirees in poor health, with limited mobility, or leading sedentary lives, underscoring the role of physical well-being (Chen & Liu, 2023)..
text.formatted: Negative experiences were often tied to feelings of isolation and distress, especially among retirees in poor health, with limited mobility, or leading sedentary lives, underscoring the role of physical well-being <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Chen & Liu, 2023)</ref>..

text.text: Prolonged negative experiences of solitude can, in turn, diminish well-being and happiness in retirement RQ2.
Subjective Norms: Negotiating Time Alone With Others Our second research question asked how people in retirees' lives influence their engagement with alone time.
In line with the subjective norms component of the TPB, family members' expectations shaped whether retirees felt able to claim time for themselves.
With a greater appreciation for their alone time, some retirees may find themselves needing to communicate this desire to others.
For some, this comes easily, but for others, social commitments with family tend to take priority, so a few mentioned that they needed to compromise.
Some participants also described feeling guilty about wanting time alone, while others noted that family members came to respect their need for personal time only gradually.

These accounts echo concerns that others may interpret older adults' solitude as loneliness (Ost-Mor et al., 2021) and that such judgments can be internalized (Nguyen et al., 2023), making retirees feel the need to justify their desire to be alone.
text.formatted: These accounts echo concerns that others may interpret older adults' solitude as loneliness <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Ost-Mor et al., 2021)</ref> and that such judgments can be internalized <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Nguyen et al., 2023)</ref>, making retirees feel the need to justify their desire to be alone.

text.text: As such, our findings extend this work by showing that norms around solitude are negotiated within the household and can shift over time.
Our third research question asked how retirees manage and use their time alone.
Consistent with the perceived behavioral control component of the TPB, participants' capacity to use solitude well depended on internal resources, such as routines and personal goals.
At the same time, being able to enjoy and engage in purposeful activities in solitude also depended on external resources, such as financial security and health.
Participants in our study expressed the desire to use solitude to pursue activities they enjoyed or to engage with personal interests, including hobbies, exercise, and various projects.

Exercise, in particular, was seen as a means of maintaining purpose and achieving personal goals during retirement, which is consistent with previous reports on retirement (Beck et al., 2010; Jonsson et al., 2000; Pettican & Prior, 2011).
text.formatted: Exercise, in particular, was seen as a means of maintaining purpose and achieving personal goals during retirement, which is consistent with previous reports on retirement <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Beck et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Jonsson et al., 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Pettican & Prior, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: By talking through things that they did or wanted to do with their time alone, the retirees in our study also engaged in the process of identifying their goals for solitude during retirement (e.g., self-reflection, self-improving activities), optimizing their experiences through their plans for solitude, as well as adapting to changes in their routine and increased amount of time alone.
According to the Selection, Optimization, and Compensation Theory (SOC) (Burnett-Wolle & Godbey, 2007), this contributes to positive aging experience.
text.formatted: According to the Selection, Optimization, and Compensation Theory (SOC) <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Burnett-Wolle & Godbey, 2007)</ref>, this contributes to positive aging experience.

text.text: The activities that retirees in our study wanted to do in their solitude are consistent with past literature suggesting that being physically active, pursuing hobbies, and maintaining a health routine have been shown to contribute to mental well-being in older adults (Mak et al., 2023; Vigezzi et al., 2025), as well as reduce risks of depression (Bone et al., 2022).
text.formatted: The activities that retirees in our study wanted to do in their solitude are consistent with past literature suggesting that being physically active, pursuing hobbies, and maintaining a health routine have been shown to contribute to mental well-being in older adults <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Mak et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">Vigezzi et al., 2025)</ref>, as well as reduce risks of depression <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bone et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: For our participants, a lot of these pursuits were tied to time spent alone, especially for those whose partners were still at work.

As such, enjoying retirement to the fullest involves planning how to use that time; this is consistent with past research suggesting that 'keeping busy' after retirement is seen to be important for 'healthy ageing' (Guell et al., 2016).
text.formatted: As such, enjoying retirement to the fullest involves planning how to use that time; this is consistent with past research suggesting that 'keeping busy' after retirement is seen to be important for 'healthy ageing' <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Guell et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Planning also meant establishing a structure during moments of solitude through learning a range of new skills and trying new experiences, which has previously showed to foster self-development (Merriam, 2005).
text.formatted: Planning also meant establishing a structure during moments of solitude through learning a range of new skills and trying new experiences, which has previously showed to foster self-development <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Merriam, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: However, building skills and engaging in activities incurred both energy and costs, therefore financial stability and good health were important for retirees to make the best of their solitude.
In retirement, financial constraints, illness or mobility issues, could restrict the options of what participants could do in their alone time.
Taken together, our findings highlight that it takes both internal and external resources for retirees to make the best of their solitude after retirement.
Finally, retirees also emphasize balancing between time for solitude and social interactions.
They appeared to be intentional about expanding their social networks, focusing on connections built around meaningful activities such as mentoring and volunteering.
A study among older adults across 26 European countries showed that having meaning in life can be a protective factor against both loneliness and depression in old ages (Nascimento et al., 2024).
text.formatted: A study among older adults across 26 European countries showed that having meaning in life can be a protective factor against both loneliness and depression in old ages <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Nascimento et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, the companionship of pets was found to alleviate loneliness by providing both emotional support and opportunities for new social interactions with other pet owners (Taniguchi et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Additionally, the companionship of pets was found to alleviate loneliness by providing both emotional support and opportunities for new social interactions with other pet owners <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">(Taniguchi et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: As such, having a balance between time spent with others and time spent alone was crucial for enjoyable solitude, consistent with existing research on the topic (Littman-Ovadia, 2019; Luo et al., 2022; Weinstein et al., 2023).
text.formatted: As such, having a balance between time spent with others and time spent alone was crucial for enjoyable solitude, consistent with existing research on the topic <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Littman-Ovadia, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Luo et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Weinstein et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Several findings from the data were not directly addressed by our research questions but help contextualize retirees' experiences of solitude.
Participants' descriptions of post-retirement changes align with previous research (Jonsson et al., 2000; Pettican & Prior, 2011).
text.formatted: Participants' descriptions of post-retirement changes align with previous research <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Jonsson et al., 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Pettican & Prior, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Accepting and adapting to these changes is an important part of this life transition, echoing previous mixed findings on retirees' well-being (Ugwu et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Accepting and adapting to these changes is an important part of this life transition, echoing previous mixed findings on retirees' well-being <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">(Ugwu et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Changes involve not only stepping away from work but also adjusting professional and social connections (Bordia et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Changes involve not only stepping away from work but also adjusting professional and social connections <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bordia et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: This shift in identity may be further reinforced by the increased alone time resulting from the loss of the structured 'working day.'
When reflecting on their retirement, retirees reassessed which relationships matter most; some decided to let go of workplace ties, while others focused on building new ones.

While a few retirees said it was challenging at the beginning to find new social connections outside of their immediate family, several adjusted through volunteering or mentoring others in their community to maintain social engagement.
These changes and adjustments align with what Socioemotional Selectivity Theory (Carstensen & Lo, 2004) suggests would be expected during this stage of life.
text.formatted: These changes and adjustments align with what Socioemotional Selectivity Theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Carstensen & Lo, 2004)</ref> suggests would be expected during this stage of life.

text.text: The theory proposes that as people get older, they adjust their priorities in both social relationships and goal pursuits.

Retirees in our study appeared to modify their social networks in ways that enhance the quality of their leisure time after retirement, even if that meant letting go of some ties and forming new ones.
For older adults, having a high-quality network is also associated with more positive experiences of solitude (Pauly et al., 2018).
text.formatted: For older adults, having a high-quality network is also associated with more positive experiences of solitude <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Pauly et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: This research adds to existing understanding of thoughts and experiences around solitude in retirement.

Our definition of solitude, provided to participants, referred to time spent not interacting with others, a momentary state rather than the structural lack of social contact that characterizes social isolation (Nguyen & Rodriguez, 2024).
text.formatted: Our definition of solitude, provided to participants, referred to time spent not interacting with others, a momentary state rather than the structural lack of social contact that characterizes social isolation <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Nguyen & Rodriguez, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Because all participants lived with others, their accounts reflect time alone within an otherwise socially connected life rather than objective isolation.
We intentionally did not specify whether time alone was chosen or unchosen, so as to capture the full range of participants' experiences.
As a result, some participants' descriptions of the risks of solitude, such as feeling disconnected or lonely, may reflect experiences that approach isolation.
Future research could examine how these experiences differ among retirees who live alone or have limited social networks.
All of our participants also reported good or very good physical health, and most had higher life satisfaction.
As such this sample may therefore not reflect the full range of retirement experiences, particularly for those in poorer physical or psychological health.
Additionally, participants were aged 58 to 66.

At the time of data collection in 2023, the UK State Pension could be claimed from age 66, and the average age of leaving the labour market was around 65 for men and 64 for women (Department for Work and Pensions, 2024).

Fourteen of our 15 retired participants had therefore retired before State Pension age, suggesting that they may have had other resources to rely on before reaching 66, such as private pensions, savings, or a spouse's earnings (Cribb, 2023).
text.formatted: Fourteen of our 15 retired participants had therefore retired before State Pension age, suggesting that they may have had other resources to rely on before reaching 66, such as private pensions, savings, or a spouse's earnings <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Cribb, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Their retirement might also be more intentional; their experiences may therefore differ from those who retire later, rely primarily on the State Pension, or who are more reluctant to retire.
Future research could also explore the perspectives of older adults who have been retired for many years to see how views and experiences change over time.

Further study into how different types of retirement and life situations shape retirees' alone time would be valuable, and could inform services offering help, advice, and support to people planning for or already in retirement.
Retirement is a multifaceted experience that brings both benefits and challenges.

While stepping away from work can enrich the lives of older adults by providing increased autonomy and more time to engage in meaningful activities, it also presents difficulties, including changes in social relationships, the loss of work structure, financial concerns, and risks of boredom and loneliness.
Participants described solitude as both a positive and negative force in retirement, often within the same individual.
Participants valued time alone for reflection, authenticity, and personal growth, yet also recognized its potential to lead to isolation, purposelessness, and negative rumination.

Retirement did not automatically grant freedom for or ownership over solitude; retirees had to negotiate boundaries with family and former colleagues to protect their time, and build new routines to replace the structure work once provided.

Stable routines, purposeful social engagement, financial security, and good health appeared to protect against the more negative aspects of solitude, shaping whether time alone felt like freedom or a constraint.

Finally, our findings suggest that how retirees engage with solitude is shaped not only by their personal evaluations of time alone but also by others' expectations about their availability, and by the practical resources that allow them to use their time in ways they choose, whether alone or with other people.

Each sub-theme is placed under the TPB component it most closely reflects, although several also touch on other components.

For example, embracing newfound freedom reflects both a positive evaluation of retirement (attitudes) and autonomy over one's time (perceived control), and guilt about wanting time alone shows how others' expectations (subjective norms) can shape attitudes toward solitude.

The sub-themes are also interconnected: freedom in retirement required renegotiating boundaries and building new routines, and financial security and health shaped whether retirees could use their time alone in the ways they chose.
